new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive rhythmic stress: heavy syllables ((C)VV or (C)VC, codas nasal only) are always stressed; light syllables are stressed on an odd count from the left edge (trochaic, left-to-right), except that a light final syllable is never stressed; the strongest (primary) stress falls on the rightmost stressed syllable. Net effect: primary stress is penultimate in words ending in two light syllables (ˈna.li, ˌna.wa.ˈla.hi, ˌtau-ˈmo.ho) and final when the final syllable is heavy (ˌma.li.ˈbon).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied: all heavy syllables and alternating odd-numbered light syllables from the left carry stress; the last of these is the strongest, the others are weaker (e.g. 'lau.-'ta.fo.-'ta.fo, 'fa.li.-'fa.li.'hu.-na).
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy syllables 'throw the pattern off' (the odd-syllable count is disrupted/restarted around them); final syllable stressed only if heavy. 'If anywhere' hedges that the primary/secondary distinction is weak.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement from an SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet; examples are citation forms including suffixed and reduplicated words (hyphens mark morpheme boundaries), so the domain includes affixes/reduplicants. No statement about phrase-level prominence. Tone and length not claimed contrastive (heavy = underlyingly two syllables).
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Buhutu as spoken at Siasiada and neighbouring villages (Ataata, Gelemalaia, Hoowalai, Ipouli, Mila, Sinalili, Bolowai, Leileiyafa; outliers Sagaafo, Libalei), i.e. the language-level languoid buhu1237 itself (alt. names Bohutu, Yaleba, Buhulu, Siasiada). No dialect restriction stated.

sources.note: p.4 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': heavy syllables ((C)VV, (C)VC) always stressed; final syllable never stressed unless heavy; otherwise stress on every odd syllable counting from the first; strongest stress tends to be on the last accented syllable.
